law: COMPARE EVERY PIECE OF ART TO THE WORLD 9/4/26 — the gate ruler
format: a REFERENCE CHECK cites entries by these ids

BLDG-01.name: UNLV "Dreaming the Skyline" architecture archive
BLDG-01.teaches: real Vegas buildings from drawings to construction; a building's massing comes from its PROGRAM (what happens inside), so draw the use first and the walls around it.

BLDG-02.name: Antoine Predock's Las Vegas Library (already canon: the library district is built on it)
BLDG-02.teaches: desert civic architecture is MASS + SHADOW, sandstone and concrete; colour comes from the desert, and glazing is small and deep because of the sun.

BLDG-03.name: SLYNYRD Pixelblog catalogue (buildings series)
BLDG-03.teaches: a pixel building is drawn in three planes (front face, side face, roof) with ONE light direction; windows sit IN the wall plane on a shared grid line, never floating between floors.

BLDG-04.name: The Strip's three races (pool, sign, porte-cochere — Stefan Al)
BLDG-04.teaches: a casino is a SMALL CITY with a giant forecourt; the front is theatre and the back of house (laundry, kitchens, docks) is where the building actually works — draw both or the building is a facade.

BLDG-05.name: Structural sanity list (the 9/4 law's own words)
BLDG-05.teaches: windows sit in a wall plane; a wall meets a roof; a door is on the ground; a street meets a curb — the four checks every building cook runs before calling itself done.

CGRD-01.name: Into the Breach interface (Game UI Database)
CGRD-01.teaches: every tile state must read from silhouette and value alone at a glance; if a player has to hover to know whether ground is dangerous, the floor has failed.

CGRD-02.name: "Sacrifice cool ideas for the sake of clarity every time" (the ItB dev interview)
CGRD-02.teaches: on a tactical floor, clarity outranks beauty on every collision; a gorgeous tile that hides its walkability is a worse tile than a plain one that shows it.

CGRD-03.name: A Vegas block from the air (satellite, any residential mile)
CGRD-03.teaches: at house-per-tile scale the ground alphabet is HOUSE / YARD / STREET / LOT and almost nothing else; a backyard is as big as its house (the 9/4 1x2 ruling is what the air actually shows).

DIST-01.name: SimCity 2000 building sprites
DIST-01.teaches: at map zoom a district reads by SILHOUETTE and ROOF PATTERN, not by wall detail; every sprite sits on the 2:1 isometric diamond and never breaks its own tile bounds.

DIST-02.name: Learning From Las Vegas (Venturi/Scott Brown)
DIST-02.teaches: a Vegas commercial plot is SIGN + SHED + PARKING IN FRONT; the building hides behind its lot, so a district that puts the building on the street edge is drawn from the wrong city.

DIST-03.name: Las Vegas aerial (any mapping satellite view)
DIST-03.teaches: a Sun Belt subdivision is a CUL-DE-SAC BULB ringed by one continuous block wall; an industrial plot is one big roof plus yard; the grain of the valley is the arterial mile grid.

DIST-04.name: Stardew Valley town map (extracted sheets)
DIST-04.teaches: in 3/4 top-down a building is FRONT FACE + ROOF BAND stacked, the door always touches the ground row, and paths read because they are one value lighter than the grass, not a different hue.

DIST-05.name: Faux urbanism on the Strip (Themerica)
DIST-05.teaches: real urban texture is LAYERED BY TIME (mismatched frontages, patched surfaces); a district where every building matches reads as a theme park, which is the exact wrongness Bohemia's dead world must avoid.

FACE-01.name: Portraits — Pedro Medeiros (saint11)
FACE-01.teaches: at portrait scale the eyes carry the face; one pixel of eye spacing changes identity more than any amount of shading.

FACE-02.name: The vertical thirds (classical construction, any figure-drawing text)
FACE-02.teaches: hairline-brow, brow-nose, nose-chin are equal thirds; the eye line is halfway down the skull; a face that breaks the thirds reads as a caricature whether you meant it or not.

FACE-03.name: The repo's own face law (identity at 64px)
FACE-03.teaches: identity at small sizes is SIZE AND SPACING, not detail — the same channel face recognition uses; cheeks widest, jaw inside them, chin inside the jaw.

GARM-01.name: Lospec clothing tutorials (curated)
GARM-01.teaches: at sprite scale fabric is VALUE BANDS, not drawn fold lines; one shadow band under every overhang (hem, cuff, collar) is what makes cloth read as layered.

GARM-02.name: Pixel Logic, ch. readability + anti-aliasing (Michael Azzi)
GARM-02.teaches: a garment's silhouette must read at 100% zoom with no outline help; interior detail that breaks the silhouette read is subtraction, not addition.

GARM-03.name: The wardrobe's own locked laws
GARM-03.teaches: a garment costs something to wear (the heat) or it signals nothing; the cut belongs to the register, the colour belongs to the faction — a cook never spends both channels on one idea.

HAIR-01.name: Pedro Medeiros (saint11) tutorials — hair and character heads
HAIR-01.teaches: hair is ONE MASS with a silhouette, clumps drawn as little off shapes; single-strand lines at sprite scale read as scratches, not hair.

HAIR-02.name: The repo's own hair laws (the deepest reference we hold)
HAIR-02.teaches: the hairline crosses the FOREHEAD, TEMPLE and EAR in profile; a haircut is one haircut from all eight directions; no straight runs longer than six rows.

HAIR-03.name: Real barbering taxonomy (any barber's chart)
HAIR-03.teaches: every real cut is LENGTH ON TOP x LENGTH ON SIDES x HOW IT FALLS; naming a cook against that grid catches a shape that is not actually a haircut anybody has.

PROP-01.name: SLYNYRD Pixelblog catalogue (props and objects series)
PROP-01.teaches: a prop is SILHOUETTE FIRST; its ground shadow is what anchors it to the world, and a prop with no contact shadow floats however well it is drawn.

PROP-02.name: Real object typology (manufacturer photos of the actual thing)
PROP-02.where: search the real object by name (a 500-gallon propane tank, a CRAC unit, a guyed mast)
PROP-02.teaches: real utility objects are ONE material and TWO or three readable parts (tank + saddle + valve); a prop cook that invents a fourth part is decorating, not observing.

PROP-03.name: The 45-degree law (ours, locked)
PROP-03.teaches: every prop is seen from the world's three-quarter view — ellipse cross-sections, visible sky-lit tops; a flat side-on prop is from a different game.

UI-01.name: Into the Breach (Interface In Game gallery)
UI-01.teaches: the game states everything it is about to do before it does it; a UI that makes the player remember instead of recognise is spending working memory the fight needs (our day-17 rule: words for the world, ONE number).

UI-02.name: Game UI principles (Kukshtel)
UI-02.teaches: UI is a conversation with one voice: every panel that invents its own layout grammar makes the player relearn the screen.

UI-03.name: The phone itself (Apple Human Interface Guidelines, touch targets)
UI-03.teaches: a touch target is 44pt minimum and the thumb lives at the bottom; anything he must reach for at the top of a portrait screen is a desktop habit wearing a phone costume.

WALK-01.name: Walk Cycle — Pedro Medeiros (saint11)
WALK-01.teaches: a sprite walk is CONTACT-DOWN-PASS-UP; the head bobs one pixel on pass, and losing the bob kills the weight before anything else does.

WALK-02.name: Walk Cycles — Sandy Gordon
WALK-02.teaches: at small sizes arms read by their SWING SILHOUETTE, not their pixels; opposite arm to leg or the walk reads as a march.

WALK-03.name: The Animator's Survival Kit (Richard Williams)
WALK-03.teaches: the walk is a controlled fall; the body is always leaving balance and catching it, so a cycle where the torso never leans is a treadmill, not a walk.
